Same trap as the sibling Final cluster: no native PDF text layer (Microsoft Lens scan), `pagetext.mjs ocr --pages 1-5` recovered the text, and the correct option on every keyed SBA carries a corrupted-glyph, circled, or margin-letter mark, confirmed by `render --force` on pages 2-5. Q6 (no mark on any option) is held as held-no-printed-key; Q18 (two conflicting marks — a circle on one option, a different margin letter on another) is held as held-indefensible-key; Q10 and Q31 are held as duplicate-of msk-final24-q15 and msk-final24-q36 respectively (same fact already authored from the Final paper, with a conflicting marked key here); Q32 is held as duplicate-of msk-final24-q35 (same isotonic/isometric-tension concept, conflicting key); Q35 is held as held-indefensible-key (asserts a triad structure contradicting this cluster's own Q22 key on the identical fact). The 9 structured-essay questions in the same paper are not authored (no single-letter key).

questions.title: Nerve paralysed in inability to invert the foot
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy is unable to invert his foot. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be paralyzed?

explanations.A: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper circles the superficial peroneal nerve for a case of inability to invert the foot. Reviewers should note this runs against the standard teaching that active inversion is produced by tibialis anterior (deep peroneal nerve) and tibialis posterior (tibial nerve), while the superficial peroneal nerve instead supplies the evertors, peroneus longus and brevis — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.B: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard teaching would instead point here, since the deep peroneal nerve supplies tibialis anterior, a prime invertor of the foot — but the paper marks superficial peroneal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral plantar nerve is a branch of the tibial nerve supplying intrinsic foot muscles and sensation to the lateral sole, not a nerve classically tied to ankle inversion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The medial plantar nerve, also a tibial nerve branch, supplies intrinsic foot muscles and sensation to the medial sole, not a nerve classically tied to ankle inversion.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the nerve paralysed in inability to invert the foot, while flagging the conflict with standard deep-peroneal/tibialis-anterior teaching.

questions.title: The axis of the foot
questions.question: The axis of the foot is a line that passes through which of the following toes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The big (first) toe abducts away from and adducts toward the foot's reference axis; it does not define the axis itself.
explanations.B: Correct. Toe abduction and adduction are described relative to a reference line through the second toe, the long axis of the foot — the lower-limb counterpart to the hand's own middle-finger axis. Toes moving away from this line are abducting, toward it are adducting, and the second toe itself is conventionally treated as having no abduction/adduction of its own. This is a frequently tested contrast with the hand, whose reference digit is the middle (third) finger, not a numerically equivalent digit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third toe abducts away from and adducts toward the reference axis through the second toe; it does not define the axis itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fourth toe abducts away from and adducts toward the reference axis through the second toe; it does not define the axis itself.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that the axis of the foot for toe abduction/adduction passes through the second toe, contrasting it with the hand's middle-finger axis.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-104 > Musculoskeletal & Integumentary > Foot terms of movement

questions.title: Artery tested in posterior leg compartment ischaemia
questions.question: An elder suffers from a vaso-occlusive disorder that affects blood supply of the posterior compartment of his leg. Which of the following arteries would you expect the doctor must test?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The medial plantar artery is a foot-sole branch of the posterior tibial artery, distal to and not itself the main supply of the posterior leg compartment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral plantar artery, likewise a foot-sole branch of the posterior tibial artery, is not the main posterior-leg-compartment vessel being tested here.
explanations.C: Correct. The peroneal artery, a branch of the posterior tibial artery, is the leg's main arterial supply and runs within the posterior compartment. It also serves as the fibula's own nutrient artery. A vaso-occlusive disorder affecting that compartment's blood supply would therefore implicate the peroneal artery among these four choices.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The circumflex fibular artery is a small genicular-region branch near the knee, not the principal vessel supplying the posterior leg compartment.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: Name the peroneal artery as the leg's main arterial supply, running through the posterior compartment as a branch of the posterior tibial artery.

questions.title: Muscle damaged in inability to unlock the knee
questions.question: A 22-year-old patient is unable to unlock the knee joint to allow flexion of the leg. Which of the following muscles is most likely damaged?

explanations.A: Correct. Popliteus unlocks the fully extended, screw-home-locked knee by laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia, or medially rotating the tibia on the fixed femur. This unlocking must happen before the hamstrings can flex the knee at all. Damage to popliteus therefore specifically blocks the ability to initiate flexion from full extension.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Biceps femoris is a hamstring that flexes the already-unlocked knee; it plays no role in the initial unlocking step.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gastrocnemius, though it crosses the knee and contributes a small flexor action, is not the muscle responsible for unlocking the screw-home-locked extended knee.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Semitendinosus, like biceps femoris, is a hamstring that flexes the already-unlocked knee, not the unlocking muscle itself.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that popliteus unlocks the fully extended knee before the hamstrings can flex it, so its damage blocks the initiation of knee flexion.

questions.title: Movement affected by ischial tuberosity fracture
questions.question: A fracture to the ischial tuberosity would affect which of the following movements of the lower limb?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thigh abduction is produced by gluteus medius/minimus (superior gluteal nerve), muscles arising from the ilium, not the ischial tuberosity.
explanations.B: Correct. The three hamstring muscles (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris) all arise from the ischial tuberosity. All three also flex the knee, as well as extending the hip. A fracture at their shared origin therefore disrupts that attachment and impairs knee flexion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thigh flexion is chiefly produced by iliopsoas, sartorius and rectus femoris, none of which arise from the ischial tuberosity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Knee extension is produced by quadriceps femoris, arising from the ilium and femoral shaft, not the ischial tuberosity.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that the hamstrings arise from the ischial tuberosity and flex the knee, so a fracture there impairs knee flexion.

questions.title: Brachial plexus part supplying skin of the lateral forearm
questions.question: Which part of the brachial plexus supplies the skin of the lateral side of the forearm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The medial cord gives rise to the medial cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm, supplying the medial, not lateral, forearm skin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lower trunk is a proximal brachial plexus element that contributes to the medial cord; it does not itself carry a discrete cutaneous branch to the forearm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The upper trunk is a proximal element contributing to the lateral and posterior cords; it does not itself carry a discrete cutaneous branch to the forearm.
explanations.D: Correct. The musculocutaneous nerve leaves the lateral cord and pierces coracobrachialis. Beyond that muscle it continues as a purely cutaneous nerve, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, supplying the skin of the lateral forearm. This makes the lateral cord the correct brachial plexus element for this territory.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that the lateral cord, via the musculocutaneous nerve's cutaneous continuation, supplies the skin of the lateral forearm.

questions.title: Function lost after posterior interosseous nerve injury
questions.question: A 33-year-old male with a gunshot wound that severely affects the forearm, injuring the posterior interosseous nerve. Which function was lost?

options.A: Putting the forearm in mid-prone position

explanations.A: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks the mid-prone forearm position as the function lost. Reviewers should note this runs against the standard posterior-interosseous-nerve picture (finger drop with wrist extension retained via extensor carpi radialis longus, and no role in pronation/supination) — see the concept's own uncertainty note and the related pending concept CON-MSK-1FC89E36FFD98E.
explanations.B: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard teaching would instead expect wrist extension to be largely retained after an isolated posterior interosseous nerve injury, since extensor carpi radialis longus is supplied above the point of division — but the paper marks option A.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Elbow extension (triceps) is supplied by the radial nerve proper well above the posterior interosseous nerve's own branch point, so it is not the deficit tested here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thumb opposition is produced by opponens pollicis, a median-nerve-supplied thenar muscle, unrelated to the posterior interosseous nerve.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the function lost after posterior interosseous nerve injury, while flagging the conflict with the standard finger-drop/wrist-extension-retained picture.

field_notes.optionD: The source page prints only three options (a-c) for this item, confirmed by render --force — a genuine 3-option question in the paper. Option D ("Opposition of the thumb") is this lane's own added distractor, not printed in the source, needed to fill the bank's standard 4-option SBA format; it targets a different, unrelated nerve territory (median) so it does not compete with the paper's own three choices.

questions.title: Ligament injured in a medial-side elbow dislocation
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy has a dislocation of his elbow joint. On MRI examination the physician reveals injury to a triangular shaped ligament on the medial side of the joint. Which of the following ligaments is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The annular ligament encircles the head of the radius at the proximal radioulnar joint; it is not the triangular medial-side ligament described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The transverse humeral ligament bridges the two humeral tuberosities anteriorly, over the bicipital groove, not the medial side of the elbow joint.
explanations.C: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks the radial collateral ligament. Reviewers should note this runs against standard elbow anatomy, in which the medial-side triangular ligament is conventionally the ulnar collateral ligament, with the radial collateral ligament instead lying laterally — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.D: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard anatomy would instead point here, since the ulnar (medial) collateral ligament is the triangular band on the medial side of the elbow — but the paper marks option C.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the triangular ligament injured on the medial side of a dislocated elbow, while flagging the conflict with standard collateral-ligament laterality.

questions.title: Muscle retaining function after a median nerve injury at the wrist
questions.question: A 24-year-old male had his median nerve injured in an industrial accident at the wrist. Which of the following muscles would still retain its function?

options.A: Lumbricals of index and middle finger
options.C: Lumbricals of ring and little finger

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lumbricals of the index and middle fingers are median-supplied and are lost with a median nerve injury at the wrist.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Abductor pollicis brevis is wholly supplied by the median nerve's recurrent branch and is lost outright with this injury.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lumbricals of the ring and little fingers are indeed ulnar-supplied and spared — but this option is not the paper's marked answer, and flexor pollicis brevis is the more specific fact tested here.
explanations.D: Correct. Flexor pollicis brevis has a superficial head that is median-supplied and a deep head that, in most hands, is instead supplied by the ulnar nerve's deep branch. The muscle can therefore retain partial function via its ulnar-supplied deep head after an isolated median nerve injury at the wrist. This distinguishes it from abductor pollicis brevis and the index/middle lumbricals, which are wholly median-supplied and lost outright.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that flexor pollicis brevis' ulnar-supplied deep head lets it retain partial function after a median nerve injury at the wrist.

questions.title: Wrist deficit from a sixth extensor compartment mass
questions.question: A localized mass compresses the sixth compartment of the extensor retinaculum. Which of the following conditions may result in the wrist joint?

explanations.A: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks weakness of flexion. Reviewers should note the sixth extensor compartment holds only extensor carpi ulnaris, so standard teaching would instead expect a wrist extension (not flexion) deficit — see the concept's own uncertainty note and the sibling fifth-compartment concept CON-MSK-9F295DCA61C8E6.
explanations.B: Not the paper's marked answer, and also inconsistent with the extensor-compartment mechanism, since flexor tendons run through the separate flexor retinaculum region unaffected by an extensor compartment mass.
explanations.C: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard teaching would instead expect a degree of extension loss from entrapment of extensor carpi ulnaris, the sixth compartment's sole tenant — but the paper marks option A.
explanations.D: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard teaching would instead point here (weakness, not loss, of extension) as the closest textbook deficit — but the paper marks option A.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the deficit from a sixth extensor compartment mass, while flagging the conflict with the extensor-carpi-ulnaris-only compartment anatomy.

questions.title: Sign expected positive in cubital tunnel syndrome
questions.question: A 23-year-old girl suffers from cubital tunnel syndrome. Which of the following signs would you expect to be positive in this patient?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trendelenburg's sign tests hip abductor (gluteus medius/minimus, superior gluteal nerve) function, an unrelated lower-limb territory, not the ulnar nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Card test" is not the standard eponymous test for ulnar nerve dysfunction in this context; Froment's sign is the recognised card-pinch test.
explanations.C: Correct. Cubital tunnel syndrome compresses the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow. Froment's sign tests adductor pollicis (ulnar-supplied): asked to pinch a card between thumb and index finger, a patient with ulnar weakness substitutes flexor pollicis longus (median-supplied), producing exaggerated thumb interphalangeal flexion. This makes Froment's sign the test that specifically probes the ulnar nerve territory affected by cubital tunnel syndrome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Hand of benediction" describes the posture from a proximal median nerve injury, not an ulnar nerve sign.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that Froment's sign, reflecting adductor pollicis weakness, is the test expected positive in cubital tunnel syndrome.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-104 > Musculoskeletal & Integumentary > Elbow and forearm nerve injuries

questions.title: Bony landmark spared in a severe elbow injury
questions.question: A 25-year-old male in a car accident severely affects the elbow joint. Which of the following bony landmarks is spared?

options.B: Upper surface of head of radius

explanations.A: Incorrect. The trochlea of the ulna forms part of the elbow joint's own articulating surface and is classically damaged in a severe elbow injury.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The upper surface of the head of the radius articulates with the capitulum and is likewise part of the joint's own articulating surface, classically damaged.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The capitulum of the humerus is one of the two humeral articular surfaces forming the elbow joint and is classically damaged.
explanations.D: Correct. The radial tuberosity, the biceps brachii insertion, sits on the radial shaft distal to the radial head. It does not itself form part of the elbow joint's articulating surface. A severe elbow joint injury classically damages the trochlea, capitulum and the radial head's own articulating surface, so the radial tuberosity is expected to be spared.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that the radial tuberosity, lying distal to the joint's own articulating surfaces, is spared in a severe elbow injury.

questions.title: Vein draining into the axillary vein
questions.question: Which of the following veins drains into the axillary vein?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The basilic vein does not "drain into" the axillary vein as a tributary — it continues directly as the axillary vein at the lower border of teres major.
explanations.B: Correct. The cephalic vein runs laterally up the arm. It terminates by piercing the clavipectoral fascia near the deltopectoral groove, joining (draining into) the axillary vein there. Among the options given, it is the one that is genuinely a tributary of the axillary vein rather than a continuation of it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The median cubital vein is a superficial connector at the elbow between the cephalic and basilic veins; it does not itself drain into the axillary vein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Medial vein of forearm" is not a standard named tributary of the axillary vein.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that the cephalic vein drains into the axillary vein, distinguishing it from the basilic vein, which continues as it.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-104 > Musculoskeletal & Integumentary > Upper limb veins

questions.title: Condition secondary to a fibular-neck common peroneal nerve injury
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy comes to hospital after a motorcycle accident which injures the neck of the fibula, with the nerve wrapped around the neck. Which of the following conditions may occur secondary to this injury?

options.B: Loss of plantarflexion of the ankle joint
options.C: Loss of sensation on the medial side of the big toe
options.D: Loss of sensation on the medial side of the foot

explanations.A: Incorrect. Talipes calcaneo-valgus is a congenital foot deformity, not a documented acute deficit of common peroneal nerve injury.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plantarflexion is produced by the tibial-nerve-supplied posterior compartment, unaffected by a common peroneal nerve injury, which instead classically costs dorsiflexion.
explanations.C: Correct. A fracture of the neck of the fibula injures the common peroneal nerve, which wraps directly around that neck. Its deep peroneal branch is reduced, sensorially, to a small patch over the first web space between the big and second toes — the closest sensory deficit among the options to the nerve's own cutaneous territory.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sensation on the medial side of the foot is saphenous nerve territory (a branch of the femoral nerve), not common peroneal territory.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that a fibular-neck fracture injures the common peroneal nerve, whose deep branch's sensory loss is confined to the first web space of the foot.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-104 > Musculoskeletal & Integumentary > Common peroneal nerve

questions.title: Muscle group affected by compression of the anterior division of L2-4
questions.question: A 35-year-old patient has a large schwannoma that compresses the anterior division of the ventral rami of L2, L3, L4. Which of the following groups of lower limb muscles is severely affected?

explanations.A: Correct. The anterior divisions of the L2-4 ventral rami form the obturator nerve. It passes through the obturator canal and supplies the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh. A schwannoma compressing these anterior divisions would therefore severely affect the medial muscle group.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior thigh/leg compartments are supplied chiefly by the sciatic nerve's tibial division and posterior divisions of the lumbosacral plexus, not the anterior division of L2-4.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The anterior thigh compartment is supplied by the femoral nerve, which arises from the posterior divisions of L2-4, the opposite division from the one compressed here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. No major lower-limb muscle group is defined as "lateral" in this compartment scheme in a way supplied by the anterior division of L2-4.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior division of the L2-4 ventral rami forms the obturator nerve, supplying the medial thigh compartment.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-104 > Musculoskeletal & Integumentary > Thigh nerve supply

questions.title: Foot action weakened by tendo-achillis rupture
questions.question: A football player tears his tendo-achillis. You would expect to find weakness in which of the following actions of the foot?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dorsiflexion is produced by the anterior compartment (deep peroneal nerve), unaffected by tendo-achillis rupture.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eversion is produced by peroneus longus/brevis (superficial peroneal nerve), unaffected by tendo-achillis rupture.
explanations.C: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks inversion as the weakened action. Reviewers should note this runs against standard teaching, which attributes the tendo-achillis (gastrocnemius-soleus) to plantarflexion, not inversion — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.D: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard teaching would instead point here, since gastrocnemius and soleus, inserting via the tendo-achillis, are the prime plantarflexors — but the paper marks option C.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the action weakened by tendo-achillis rupture, while flagging the conflict with standard plantarflexion teaching.

questions.title: Artery to ligate for deep palmar arch bleeding
questions.question: A 26-year-old man suffers severe bleeding in his hand, and examination shows the bleeding is from the deep palmar arch. Which of the following arteries must be ligated to stop this bleeding?

explanations.A: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks the ulnar artery. Reviewers should note this runs against standard teaching, in which the deep palmar arch is chiefly the radial artery's own termination (completed by the ulnar artery's deep branch) — see the concept's own uncertainty note and the related pending concept CON-MSK-BC95DAE3531583.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The anterior interosseous artery supplies the deep forearm flexor compartment, not the deep palmar arch itself.
explanations.C: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard teaching would instead point here, since the deep palmar arch is chiefly the radial artery's own termination — but the paper marks option A.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior interosseous artery supplies the deep forearm extensor compartment, not the deep palmar arch itself.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the artery to ligate to stop deep palmar arch bleeding, while flagging the conflict with standard radial-artery teaching.

questions.title: Gland discharging an oily secretion into the hair follicle
questions.question: Which one of the following glands discharges an oily secretion into the lumen of hair follicles?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Apocrine sweat glands do open into hair follicles (in the axilla/groin) but produce a viscous, odorous secretion, not the classic oily one this question targets.
explanations.B: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks merocrine sweat glands. Reviewers should note this runs against standard histology, in which sebaceous glands are the ones that discharge an oily, holocrine secretion into the hair follicle lumen, while merocrine (eccrine) sweat glands secrete a watery product independently onto the skin surface — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.C: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard histology would instead point here, since sebaceous glands are defined by their oily, holocrine secretion into the hair follicle — but the paper marks option B.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Eccrine sweat glands secrete a watery product independently onto the skin surface, not an oily one into hair follicles.

questions.subject: derm
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the gland discharging an oily secretion into the hair follicle, while flagging the conflict with standard sebaceous-gland teaching.

questions.title: Description of the skeletal muscle triad
questions.question: Which of the following describes the triad in skeletal muscle?

options.A: A pair of terminal cisternae with a longitudinal tubule
options.B: A pair of terminal cisternae with a transverse tubule
options.C: A pair of terminal cisternae with an oblique tubule
options.D: A pair of transverse tubule with one terminal cisternae

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tubule component of the triad is transverse (an invagination of the sarcolemma running perpendicular to the fibre's long axis), not longitudinal.
explanations.B: Correct. The skeletal muscle triad is a single transverse (T) tubule flanked by a pair of terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, at the A-I junction of each sarcomere. Depolarisation spreading down the T-tubule is sensed by dihydropyridine receptors, mechanically coupled to ryanodine receptors on the adjacent terminal cisternae, triggering calcium release for contraction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The tubule component of the triad is transverse, not obliquely oriented.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The triad has a single transverse tubule paired with two terminal cisternae, not two transverse tubules paired with a single cisterna.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that the skeletal muscle triad is a single transverse tubule flanked by a pair of terminal cisternae.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-104 > Musculoskeletal & Integumentary > Skeletal muscle histology

questions.title: Component not seen in the muscle spindle
questions.question: In the muscle spindle, which of the following is not seen?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Annulospiral (group Ia) nerve endings are a standard afferent sensory component of the muscle spindle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Flower spray (group II) nerve endings are likewise a standard afferent sensory component of the muscle spindle.
explanations.C: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks gamma motor fibers. Reviewers should note this runs against standard physiology, in which gamma motor fibres are efferent components of the spindle, innervating its intrafusal fibres, while alpha motor fibres — supplying only extrafusal fibres outside the spindle capsule — are the ones actually absent from it. See the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.D: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard teaching would instead point here, since alpha motor fibres supply only extrafusal fibres outside the spindle — but the paper marks option C.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the component not seen in the muscle spindle, while flagging the conflict with standard alpha/gamma motor fibre teaching.

questions.title: Collagen type present in hyaline cartilage
questions.question: Which type of collagen is present in hyaline cartilage?

explanations.A: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks collagen type I. Reviewers should note this runs against standard histology, in which hyaline cartilage's matrix is built on a framework of collagen type II, while type I is bone's own collagen — see the concept's own uncertainty note and the related pending concept CON-FND-E6C216AED80ED8.
explanations.B: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard histology would instead point here, since collagen type II is the accepted hyaline cartilage collagen — but the paper marks option A.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Collagen type III is characteristic of reticular fibres (lymphoid organs, blood vessel walls), not hyaline cartilage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Collagen type IV is a basement-membrane collagen, not the fibrillar collagen of hyaline cartilage matrix.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the collagen type in hyaline cartilage, while flagging the conflict with standard type-II teaching.

questions.title: Cartilage type present in the epiphyseal plate
questions.question: What type of cartilage is present in the epiphyseal plates?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Articular cartilage is a separate, permanent cartilage covering the bone ends inside the joint, not the growth-plate cartilage between epiphysis and diaphysis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Elastic cartilage, rich in elastic fibres, is found in structures like the ear and epiglottis, not the epiphyseal plate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibrocartilage, rich in type I collagen, is found in intervertebral discs and menisci, not the epiphyseal plate.
explanations.D: Correct. The epiphyseal plate passes through a sequence of zones, beginning with a zone of resting hyaline cartilage. Later zones (proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, invasion and ossification) progressively convert that cartilage to bone. Hyaline cartilage is therefore the cartilage type that persists, along with articular cartilage, as one of the two structures not replaced by bone once ossification is otherwise complete.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that the epiphyseal plate begins as a zone of resting hyaline cartilage.

questions.title: Description of the osteoclast's basal zone
questions.question: Which of the following sentences best describes bone osteoclasts?

options.A: Basal-zone lacks organelles but contains many actin filaments
options.B: Ruffled zone is farthest away from the bone surface
options.C: Plasma membrane of the clear zone forms the sealing zone
options.D: Vesicular zone contains multiple nuclei, mitochondria and Golgi

explanations.A: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks this description of the basal zone. Reviewers should note this runs against standard histology, which attributes an organelle-poor, actin-filament-rich composition to the clear (sealing) zone, while the basal zone instead holds the nucleus and the bulk of the organelles — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ruffled border faces the bone surface directly (the resorbing surface), not farthest from it.
explanations.C: Not the paper's marked answer, though the underlying fact (the clear zone's plasma membrane seals the resorption compartment against the bone surface) is closer to standard teaching than option A — the paper nonetheless marks option A.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Multiple nuclei are a basal-zone (not vesicular-zone) feature, reflecting the osteoclast's formation by fusion of haemopoietic progenitors; the vesicular zone instead holds transport vesicles.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the osteoclast zone lacking organelles but rich in actin filaments, while flagging the conflict with standard clear-zone teaching.

questions.title: Structure that is not part of the nail
questions.question: Which of the following is not a structural part of the nail?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hyponychium, the thickened epidermis beneath the free edge of the nail plate, is a genuine nail structure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The eponychium (cuticle), the fold of skin overlapping the proximal nail plate, is a genuine nail structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lunula, the pale crescent at the base of the nail plate marking the visible part of the nail matrix, is a genuine nail structure.
explanations.D: Correct. The glassy (vitreous) membrane is a hair-follicle structure, forming the innermost layer of the outer root sheath's basement-membrane region. It has no counterpart in the nail apparatus. Among these four options, it is therefore the one that is not a structural part of the nail.

questions.subject: derm
questions.learning_objective: State that the glassy membrane, a hair-follicle structure, is not a structural part of the nail.

questions.title: Correct effect on hormonal regulation of serum calcium
questions.question: Regarding hormonal regulation of serum Ca++ level, which of the following is a correct effect on Ca++?

options.D: Thyroid hormone decreases serum Ca++ level

explanations.A: Incorrect. Parathormone raises, not decreases, serum calcium, chiefly by stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption.
explanations.B: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks that calcitonin increases serum calcium. Reviewers should note this runs against standard physiology, in which calcitonin instead lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption, while glucocorticoids (option C) carry the textbook calcium-lowering effect — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.C: Not the paper's marked answer, though this statement (glucocorticoids decrease serum calcium via reduced intestinal absorption and increased renal excretion) is the one closer to standard teaching — the paper nonetheless marks option B.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thyroid hormone (T3/T4) tends to increase bone turnover and can raise, not decrease, serum calcium in excess; it is calcitonin, a separate thyroid C-cell product, that lowers calcium.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer on hormonal regulation of serum calcium, while flagging the conflict with standard calcitonin-lowers-calcium teaching.

questions.title: Mechanism of the presynaptic inhibitory potential
questions.question: Which one of the following is the mechanism of the pre-synaptic inhibitory potential?

explanations.A: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard neurophysiology would instead point here, since GABA-mediated increased chloride permeability on the presynaptic terminal (producing primary afferent depolarisation, which reduces calcium influx and transmitter release) is the accepted mechanism — but the paper marks option C.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased potassium outflux is a hyperpolarising, postsynaptic-inhibition-associated mechanism, not the standard presynaptic-inhibition pathway.
explanations.C: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks increased Na+ influx. Reviewers should note this runs against standard neurophysiology, since sodium influx is depolarising and excitatory wherever it occurs, not the accepted presynaptic-inhibition mechanism — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased calcium permeability at the presynaptic terminal would increase, not decrease, neurotransmitter release — the opposite of inhibition.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the mechanism of presynaptic inhibition, while flagging the conflict with standard chloride-permeability teaching.

questions.title: Appropriate feature of skeletal muscle contraction
questions.question: Regarding skeletal muscle, which of the following is an appropriate feature of muscle contraction?

options.A: During its occurrence, the sarcomeres lengthened
options.B: It occurs when catecholamine is released at the motor end plate
options.C: It occurs when calcium is released from the sarcotubular system
options.D: It occurs when its pacemaker cells reach the threshold for firing

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sarcomeres shorten, not lengthen, during contraction, as the thin filaments slide further over the thick filaments.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acetylcholine, not catecholamine, is the neurotransmitter released at the skeletal neuromuscular junction's motor end plate.
explanations.C: Correct. Excitation-contraction coupling relays a T-tubule depolarisation into calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum's terminal cisternae, the sarcotubular system. The released calcium then binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin off the actin binding site and permitting cross-bridge cycling. This calcium-release step is the defining trigger of skeletal muscle contraction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle fibres have no intrinsic pacemaker cells; that property belongs to cardiac and some smooth muscle, not skeletal muscle, which is instead triggered by somatic motor neuron input.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State that skeletal muscle contraction is triggered by calcium release from the sarcotubular system during excitation-contraction coupling.

questions.title: Function of troponin T
questions.question: Regarding the regulatory proteins, which of the following is the function of troponin-T?

options.B: It is a calcium binding protein
options.C: It is the binding site for the myosin cross-bridge

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inhibiting the actin-myosin interaction at rest is troponin I's function, not troponin T's.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Binding calcium and initiating contraction is troponin C's function, not troponin T's.
explanations.C: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks the myosin cross-bridge binding site as troponin T's function. Reviewers should note this runs against standard physiology, in which troponin T is instead defined by binding tropomyosin (anchoring the troponin complex to it), while the myosin cross-bridge binding site actually lies on actin itself — see the concept's own uncertainty note and the related pending concept CON-MSK-287D88DF2F6B8C.
explanations.D: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard physiology would instead point here, since troponin T's defining function is binding tropomyosin — but the paper marks option C.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for troponin T's function, while flagging the conflict with standard tropomyosin-binding teaching.

questions.title: Main energy source for muscle during the recovery period
questions.question: Regarding energy for the muscle, what is the main, unlimited and major source of energy in the period of recovery?

explanations.A: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks ATP. Reviewers should note this runs against standard physiology, in which free fatty acid oxidation, powering the recovery period's elevated oxygen consumption, is the accepted "main, unlimited" fuel source, while muscle ATP stores are small and are what recovery metabolism is busy replenishing, not drawing on — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.B: Not the paper's marked answer. Standard physiology would instead point here, since free fatty acid oxidation is the functionally unlimited fuel source powering recovery-period metabolism — but the paper marks option A.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creatine phosphate is itself a small, rapidly depleted and replenished store, not an unlimited energy source.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucose/glycogen stores, while used during recovery, are limited compared to fat stores and are not the "unlimited" answer this question targets.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer for the main, unlimited energy source during muscle recovery, while flagging the conflict with standard free-fatty-acid teaching.

questions.title: Character of skeletal muscle chronaxie compared to its nerve
questions.question: Both nerve and muscle are excitable tissues. Which one of the following is a character of skeletal muscle chronaxie?

options.A: Shorter than that of its nerve
options.C: Equal to that of its nerve
options.D: Longer than that of its nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle chronaxie is not shorter than its nerve's — muscle fibres respond more slowly than the nerve supplying them.
explanations.B: Correct per this paper's marked key. The paper marks that skeletal muscle chronaxie is variable compared to its nerve. Reviewers should note that standard teaching instead makes the specific claim that normally-innervated skeletal muscle chronaxie is longer than that of its nerve, a fact this paper's own key states only vaguely — see the concept's own uncertainty note.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle chronaxie is not equal to its nerve's; the two excitable tissues have characteristically different chronaxie values.
explanations.D: Not the paper's marked answer, though this specific, standard-teaching comparison (muscle chronaxie longer than its nerve's) is the more precise textbook statement — the paper nonetheless marks the vaguer option B.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: State the paper's own marked answer comparing skeletal muscle chronaxie to its nerve, while flagging the conflict with the standard longer-than-its-nerve teaching.
